actions.amber: Step up resistance exercise and review calcium and vitamin D with the doctor.
actions.red: Tell the flight surgeon; consider medication to protect the bone.

bone.effect: Without gravity, bones lose mass. With resistance exercise, most people return from 6 months on the ISS with a loss under 5% at the hip and spine.
bone.how: Bone densitometry (DXA), done before and after flight.

actions.amber: Repeat in 15 min. Below 90: hydrate and sit or lie down before standing. Between 120 and 139: cut salt and keep exercising.
actions.green: Keep up daily exercise and hydration.
actions.red: Repeat the measurement; if confirmed, tell the flight surgeon. Above 180, or with chest pain, shortness of breath or a change in vision: emergency.

bp.effect: Without gravity the heart and vessels adapt and the heart can become rounder. Back in gravity, pressure can drop (risk of dizziness and fainting).
bp.how: Blood pressure cuff on the arm, seated and at rest for 5 min.

actions.amber: Finish the time on the same day; prioritise resistance exercise.
actions.green: Keep going. Show the streak of days completed.
actions.red: Re-plan the schedule with the ground team to recover the sessions.

exer.effect: On the ISS, the average loss of strength and aerobic fitness is 10 to 12%. Sessions over 20 min with a heart rate above 70% of maximum reduced the loss.
exer.how: Automatic log from the equipment, or a note in the app.

actions.amber: Repeat fasting the next day and review the diet.
actions.red: 15/15 rule: eat 15 g of fast carbohydrate and measure again in 15 min. If it does not rise, or with confusion or fainting: emergency.

gluc.effect: Food, sleep and exercise change the metabolic routine on board.
gluc.frequency: Weekly, or with symptoms (shaking, sweating, confusion)

actions.amber: Increase the load or frequency of resistance exercise.
actions.red: Tell the flight surgeon and re-plan the exercise routine.

grip.effect: In microgravity muscles lose mass and strength; losses of up to 20% do not stop the mission and can be recovered after flight.
grip.how: Strength test on the resistance exercise equipment, compared with the test before flight.

actions.amber: Check for poor sleep, stress, caffeine or fever. Repeat after 10 min of rest.
actions.red: Record an ECG if equipment is available and tell the flight surgeon. With chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath: emergency.

hr.effect: The same cardiovascular adaptations as blood pressure. Well-trained people can have a normal rate below 60.
hr.how: Watch, heart-rate strap or ECG, on waking, before getting up.

actions.amber: Suggest self-care: journal, look out the window, tend the plants, a moment of privacy, contact with family.
actions.red: Refer to a private conversation with the psychologist or the flight surgeon.

mood.effect: Isolation, confinement, radiation and distance from Earth can affect mental health.
mood.how: Daily question in the app: 'How are you today?' (1 = very bad, 5 = very good).

actions.amber: Spend less time in less shielded areas and plan EVAs with the radiation team.
actions.red: Tell the flight surgeon and the radiation team; review the activities left in the mission.

radiation.effect: Space radiation raises the lifetime risk of cancer; the career limit keeps the excess risk of death from cancer under 3%.
radiation.how: Personal dosimeter, adding up every mission.

actions.amber: Use lighting that imitates day and night, avoid caffeine in the afternoon and protect bedtime.
actions.red: Tell the flight surgeon and do not schedule critical tasks (EVA, manoeuvres) until sleep recovers, especially between 1 and 7 AM on the body clock.

sleep.effect: On the ISS there are 16 sunrises a day, which scrambles the body clock; there is also overwork and irregular schedules.
sleep.how: Actigraphy watch, or a log on waking.

actions.amber: Measure again with the hand warm and still (the oximeter is off by 2 to 4%). At 92 or below, tell the flight surgeon.
actions.red: Immediate care: supplemental oxygen per protocol and the flight surgeon.

spo2.effect: Future spacecraft will have a reduced-pressure cabin, which raises the risk of mild hypoxia: confusion, headache, changes in vision and poor sleep.
spo2.frequency: Daily, and before and after a spacewalk (EVA)

actions.amber: Hydrate, rest and measure again in 4 h. Note any other symptoms.
actions.red: Tell the flight surgeon. Isolate from the crew if an infection is suspected.

temp.effect: The immune system changes in space; astronauts have had cold sores, atypical allergies, skin rashes and infections from reactivated latent viruses.
temp.frequency: Daily, and whenever you feel unwell

actions.amber: Keep to microgravity EVAs; step up aerobic training before any surface EVA.
actions.red: Postpone planned EVAs, increase aerobic training and tell the flight surgeon.

vo2.effect: Without gravity the heart and muscles work less; aerobic capacity can fall by 10% to 30% after flight.
vo2.how: Exercise test on the cycle ergometer, measured directly or estimated from heart rate.

brain.space: Isolation, confinement, noise and shifted light cycles erode sleep, mood and focus. NASA lists behavioural health among the top risks of long missions.

eyes.space: Fluids shift toward the head in 0 g. After months, some astronauts develop swelling at the back of the eye (SANS). A weekly Amsler grid is a quick screen.

gut.space: Appetite falls, food is packaged and the gut microbiome shifts. Weight loss is common on long missions.

heart.space: Without gravity the heart works less and blood volume drops. Back under gravity, standing up can make you faint.

immune.space: Stress, radiation and confinement change immune cells. Latent viruses can wake up. Lymphocytes are among the first cells to drop after radiation.

kidneys.space: Bone mineral ends up in urine and thirst fades, which raises the risk of kidney stones.

lungs.space: Cabin air is recycled. Carbon dioxide builds up faster than on Earth and dust on the Moon and Mars is fine and sharp.

muscles.space: Leg and back muscles shrink fast without load. Daily resistive exercise is the main defence.

skeleton.space: Weight-bearing bones lose mineral in 0 g, on the order of 1% a month without countermeasures. Resistive exercise slows it.

skin.space: Outside Earth's magnetic field, galactic cosmic rays and solar storms add dose every day. The total is tracked against a career limit.

brain.space: Isolation, confinement, noise and shifted light cycles erode sleep, mood and focus. NASA lists behavioural health among the top risks of long missions.

eyes.space: Fluids shift toward the head in 0 g. After months, some astronauts develop swelling at the back of the eye (SANS). A weekly Amsler grid is a quick screen.

gut.space: Appetite falls, food is packaged and the gut microbiome shifts. Weight loss is common on long missions.

heart.space: Without gravity the heart works less and blood volume drops. Back under gravity, standing up can make you faint.

immune.space: Stress, radiation and confinement change immune cells. Latent viruses can wake up. Lymphocytes are among the first cells to drop after radiation.

kidneys.space: Bone mineral ends up in urine and thirst fades, which raises the risk of kidney stones.

lungs.space: Cabin air is recycled. Carbon dioxide builds up faster than on Earth and dust on the Moon and Mars is fine and sharp.

muscles.space: Leg and back muscles shrink fast without load. Daily resistive exercise is the main defence.

skeleton.space: Weight-bearing bones lose mineral in 0 g, on the order of 1% a month without countermeasures. Resistive exercise slows it.

skin.space: Outside Earth's magnetic field, galactic cosmic rays and solar storms add dose every day. The total is tracked against a career limit.

allergy.name: Severe allergic reaction

steps.t: Signs: swollen lips or tongue, wheezing, rash, dizziness. If in doubt, treat.
Press the epinephrine auto-injector into the outer thigh and hold for 10 seconds. Through clothing is fine.

steps.t: Give the second dose in the other thigh. Get oxygen and airway gear ready.

bleed.name: Heavy bleeding

steps.t: Gloves and goggles on. Press gauze straight onto the wound, hard, without lifting to look.
steps.variant: In 0 g blood forms a dome on the skin, then breaks into floating drops. Cover with an absorbent pad from the start.

steps.t: Hold the pressure for a full 10 minutes.

chest.name: Chest pain

steps.t: Stop everything. Put them in the most comfortable position and loosen tight clothing.
steps.variant: Tether them lightly so they spend no effort staying in place.

steps.q: Is the pain a pressure, spreading to arm or jaw, or with sweating and breathlessness?
steps.t: Measure pulse, pressure and oxygen. Run the ECG if the device is at hand.
Treat it as a heart attack until proven otherwise. Chewable aspirin from the kit if there is no allergy, per the medical protocol. Oxygen if saturation is below 94%.

steps.q: Did they pass out and stop breathing?
steps.t: Keep the defibrillator switched on beside them.
Repeat vital signs every 5 minutes and note pain from 0 to 10. Send the ECG to Earth.

choke.name: Choking

steps.t: Ask: "Are you choking?"
Tell them to cough hard and stay beside them. Do not slap the back while the cough is working.
Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades, with the person leaning forward.
steps.variant: Hook your feet under the floor loops and hold their chest with your other arm. Otherwise you both spin.

steps.t: Give 5 abdominal thrusts: fist above the navel, pull in and up.
steps.variant: Hug from behind with your legs around their waist, or with your feet anchored. All the force comes from your arms.

steps.t: Alternate 5 back blows and 5 thrusts. If they pass out, start CPR.
Keep them seated and breathing slowly. Pain or a cough that lingers after thrusts needs an exam.
steps.variant: Collect what came out. A floating fragment can be inhaled by someone else.

cpr.name: Not responding, not breathing

steps.t: Call their name and tap both shoulders hard. Watch the chest for up to 10 seconds.
Shout for help. One person fetches the defibrillator and the medical kit.
steps.variant: Move them to the restraint board and strap chest and legs. Without a rigid surface behind the back, compressions do nothing.

steps.t: Push the centre of the chest 100 to 120 times a minute, 5 to 6 cm deep. Follow the pulsing circle.
steps.variant: You have no weight. Hook your feet under the floor loops, or do the handstand method: feet on the ceiling, arms straight on the chest. Alone with no board: Evetts-Russomano method, your legs wrapped around their torso.

steps.t: After every 30 compressions give 2 breaths with the mask, if someone is trained. If not, compressions only.
Defibrillator is here: switch it on, stick the pads on the bare chest and follow its voice. Nobody touches the patient during a shock.
steps.variant: Check that nobody is floating against the patient or the board.

steps.t: Swap the person doing compressions every 2 minutes. Do not stop.
Turn them on their side with the airway clear. Check pulse, pressure and oxygen every 5 minutes.
steps.variant: Keep them strapped, on their side. Vomit does not drain in 0 g: keep suction ready.

crisis.name: Emotional crisis

steps.t: Stay with them. Speak slowly, in short sentences. Move to a place with less noise and light.
Breathe together: in while the circle grows, out while it shrinks. Two minutes.
Ask them to name 5 things they see, 4 they can touch, 3 they hear. It brings them back to now.

steps.q: Ask directly: "Have you thought about hurting yourself?" Was the answer yes?
steps.t: Asking does not put the idea in anyone’s head. It protects.
Do not leave them alone. Lock away medication and sharp tools. The medical officer takes over and Earth is told at top priority.
Agree on the next 24 hours: sleep, one light task and a private talk with the mission psychologist.

seizure.name: Seizure

steps.t: The timer is already running. Do not hold them down. Put nothing in their mouth.
Move them away from edges, panels and loose objects. Cushion the head.
steps.variant: Tether them loosely at the waist so they do not drift into equipment. Leave slack for the body to move.

steps.t: Loosen the collar. Notice how it started: one side or both? The doctor will ask.
Look at the timer. Most seizures stop on their own within 1 to 3 minutes.
Past 5 minutes, or a second seizure: the medical officer gives the rescue medication from the kit, at the protocol dose. Get oxygen ready.
Turn them on their side and check breathing. They will wake confused and tired. Speak softly and stay close.
steps.variant: On their side and strapped to the board. Suction and bags within reach: in 0 g vomit stays in the mouth.

steps.t: Measure glucose, oxygen, pulse and temperature. Look for a head bump or a bitten tongue.
